findings.summary: Proven by the supplied argument: for odd k under the uniform distribution on Z_k, there is a proper replicable learner with sample complexity O((log(1/δ)+1/ρ)/ε), specifically n at least max{(1/ε)log(2/δ), 12/(ερ)}. The shifted-partition accuracy argument, version-space concentration, and exact-output replicability bound are mathematically sound.

Proven in the stated regime, including against randomized, computationally unbounded, improper learners: when 0<ε≤1/4, 0<δ,ρ≤1/20, and odd k≥1/(5ερ), every learner working for all targets under the fixed uniform distribution requires n≥1/(120ερ). The mode extraction, symmetric coupling, adjacent-mode agreement bound, and long-path accuracy argument are valid.

The Θ(1/(ερ)) characterization is correct for fixed small confidence parameters, or more generally when log(2/δ)=O(1/ρ), but is overstated if δ may vary arbitrarily. For extremely small δ, the proved upper bound is governed by (1/ε)log(1/δ), and no matching confidence-dependent lower bound is supplied; this qualification does not affect the two numbered bounds themselves.

The transfer to the worst-case quantity n_rep is logically valid under the stated odd-k and parameter conditions: any learner required to work for every distribution must work for the uniform distribution on Z_k, so n_rep≥1/(120ερ). The resulting corollary is weak, has no growing log k factor, and does not improve the established headline lower bound.

The absence of an additional growing log k cost is supported only for the fixed uniform-distribution experiment, because the proper learner’s bound is independent of k for fixed ε,δ,ρ. It does not rule out greater replicable sample complexity for the same class H_k under an adversarial nonuniform distribution; the warranted conclusion is only that the uniform one-coordinate mechanism does not itself generate a growing log k factor.

The coordinatewise tensorization calculation is a plausible heuristic, not a theorem about the original multidimensional i.i.d. family. Allocating about n/d samples per coordinate suggests per-coordinate instability d/(nε), total mismatch d²/(nε), and the naive scaling n=O(d²/(ερ)); however, random coordinate counts and possible global structure prevent this calculation from establishing a multidimensional theorem.
